statement: Three boxes hold 52 marbles in all. The second box has 4 more marbles than the first. The third box has twice as many as the first. How many marbles are in the third box?

choices.misconception: I found the number in the first box, 12, and stopped.
I found the number in the second box, $12 + 4 = 16$, instead of the third.
I took the extra 4 away twice, once for the second box and once for the third, so I shared 44 into 4 bars of 11 and doubled it to get 22.
I forgot the 4 extra marbles, so I shared 52 into 4 equal bars of 13 and doubled it to get 26.

hints: Draw one bar for the first box.
Draw the first box as one bar. The second is one bar plus 4, the third is two bars. Take away the extra 4 and share what is left among the bars.
There are 4 equal bars and an extra 4. So the 4 bars make $52 - 4 = 48$, and one bar is 12.

solutions.reliable: Draw the first box as one bar. The second box is one bar and 4 more. The third box is two bars. Altogether: 4 bars and 4 marbles make 52. So 4 bars make 48 and one bar is 12. The third box has two bars: $2 \times 12 = 24$. Check: $12 + 16 + 24 = 52$. The transferable idea: draw equal bars, remove the extras, then share.

whyOnTest: Bar models make part-whole problems visual; three parts with a difference and a multiple test drawing before calculating.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
